questions.question_text:
Statements: Some rectangles are triangles; all circles are triangles.
Conclusions: I. All triangles are rectangles. II. Some rectangles are circles.
Which conclusion(s) follow?
questions.explanation: The overlap of rectangles and triangles does not make every triangle a rectangle, so I is not definite. The statements also do not require any circle to be a rectangle, so II is not definite.

questions.question_text:
Statements: Some ponds are rivers; no river is a lake; all lakes are oceans.
Conclusions: I. Some ponds are lakes. II. Some lakes are not oceans.
Which conclusion(s) follow?

options.C: 3) Neither conclusion I nor II follows
options.D: 4) Either conclusion I or II follows
options.E: 5) Both conclusions I and II follow

questions.explanation: The ponds known to be rivers cannot be lakes, and no premise requires any other pond to be a lake. Every lake is an ocean, so conclusion II contradicts the third statement. Neither conclusion follows.

questions.question_text:
Statements: All packets are envelopes; no envelope is a gift; some gifts are boxes.
Conclusions: I. Some boxes are packets. II. No packet is an envelope.
Which conclusion(s) follow?

options.A: 1) Neither conclusion I nor II follows
options.D: 4) Either conclusion I or II follows
options.E: 5) Both conclusions I and II follow

questions.explanation: The known gift-boxes are outside envelopes and therefore outside packets, but other boxes may or may not be packets. Conclusion II directly contradicts the statement that all packets are envelopes.

questions.question_text:
Statements: No pipes are bricks; some Scotty are not bricks; some masks are Scotty.
Conclusions: I. Some masks are not Scotty. II. No pipe is a mask.
Which conclusion(s) follow?
questions.explanation: The mask-Scotty overlap may lie entirely among Scotty that are bricks or entirely among those that are not; no mask outside Scotty is established. Pipes and masks have no stated relation, so they may overlap. Neither conclusion is forced.

questions.question_text:
Statements: No bucket is a lock; some bulbs are buckets.
Conclusions: I. No lock is a bulb. II. Some buckets are not bulbs.
Which conclusion(s) follow?
questions.explanation: The bulb-bucket overlap is outside locks, but locks may overlap bulbs outside buckets, so I is not forced. The stated bulbs are buckets; there is no existential evidence of a bucket outside bulbs, so II is not forced.

questions.question_text:
Statements: Some cars are trains; no train is a bike; some bikes are not trucks.
Conclusions: I. Some trucks are not bikes. II. Some bikes are not cars.
Which conclusion(s) follow?
questions.explanation: The truck set may lie wholly within bikes, so I is not guaranteed. The bikes known not to be trucks may still be cars, while other bikes could be outside cars; therefore II is also not guaranteed.

questions.question_text:
Statements: All rooms are tables; all doors are rooms; no cards are rooms.
Conclusions: I. No tables are cards. II. Some cards are not tables.
Which conclusion(s) follow?
questions.explanation: Only rooms are excluded from cards. Tables outside rooms may overlap cards, so I does not follow. No premise asserts that cards exist or that any card lies outside tables, so II does not follow.

questions.question_text:
Statements: No books are pens; some wickets are boxes; some boxes are pens.
Conclusions: I. Some boxes are not books. II. Some boxes are wickets.
Which conclusion(s) follow?
questions.explanation: The boxes that are pens cannot be books because books and pens are disjoint, proving I. “Some wickets are boxes” is equivalent to “some boxes are wickets,” proving II.

questions.question_text:
Statements: No coin is a note; some notes are dollars; only a few dollars are pounds.
Conclusions: I. All coins can be pounds. II. Some pounds are dollars.
Which conclusion(s) follow?
questions.explanation: Only a few dollars are pounds asserts that some dollars are pounds and some dollars are not pounds, so II follows. The notes that are dollars may occupy the non-pound dollar region, leaving it possible for every coin to be a pound because coins and notes are disjoint.

questions.question_text:
Statements: All A are B; some B are C; some C are D.
Conclusions: I. All A are C. II. Some A are not C.
Which conclusion(s) follow?
questions.explanation: Neither conclusion is individually forced: A may lie wholly in C, or some A may lie in B outside C while the required B-C overlap remains. The conclusions use the same terms and are complementary (all A are C versus some A are not C); both possibilities remain consistent, so the either-or result applies.

questions.question_text:
Statements: All A are B; some B are C; some C are D.
Conclusions: I. Some A are D. II. No D is A.
Which conclusion(s) follow?
questions.explanation: The required B-C and C-D overlaps may be arranged without involving A, and they may also be arranged with an A-D overlap. Thus neither conclusion is individually forced, but both are possible and form the complementary “some A are D” / “no D is A” pair. Either-or follows.

questions.question_text:
Statements: All A are B; some B are C; some C are D.
Conclusions: I. All A are D. II. No A is D.
Which conclusion(s) follow?
questions.explanation: The existential overlaps can occur outside A, so neither an A-D overlap nor complete A-D separation is required. These conclusions are not a complementary pair: partial overlap is a third possible arrangement. Neither follows.

questions.question_text:
Statements: All A are B; some B are C; some C are D.
Conclusions: I. No D is C. II. Some D are C.
Which conclusion(s) follow?
questions.explanation: “Some C are D” directly establishes that some D are C. That same overlap makes “No D is C” false. Only conclusion II follows.

questions.question_text:
Statements: All A are B; some B are C; some C are D.
Conclusions: I. All B are D. II. Some D are not B.
Which conclusion(s) follow?
questions.explanation: The B-C overlap and C-D overlap need not be the same elements, so not all B must be D. The stated C-D overlap may lie inside B or outside it, so some D outside B is not guaranteed. Neither follows.

questions.question_text:
Statements: All A are B; some B are C; some C are D.
Conclusions: I. Some A are D. II. Some A are not D.
Which conclusion(s) follow?
questions.explanation: A is only constrained to be within B; the required B-C and C-D overlaps may occur outside A. Since A need not exist, neither existential conclusion about A is forced.
